Abstract.

Given a graph GG with only even degrees let ε⁡(G)\varepsilon(G) be the number of Eulerian orientations and let h⁡(G)h(G) denote the number of half graphs, that is, subgraphs FF such that dF​(v)=dG​(v)/2d_{F}(v)=d_{G}(v)/2 for each vertex vv. Recently, M. Borbényi and P. Csikvári proved that ε⁡(G)≥h⁡(G)\varepsilon(G)\geq h(G) holds true for all Eulerian graphs with equality if and and only if GG is bipartite. In this paper we give a simple new proof of this fact, and we give identities and inequalities for the number of Eulerian orientations and half graphs of a 22-cover of a graph GG.

Key words and phrases: 
Eulerian orientations, factors, half graphs, covers
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 05C30. Secondary: 05C70, 05C76, 05C45

1. Introduction

In this paper we mostly study orientations and special subgraphs of Eulerian graphs. Recall that a graph GG is Eulerian if each vertex of GG has even degree. In the literature it is often assumed that an Eulerian graph is also connected, but we will not require connectedness in this paper. Let ε⁡(G)\varepsilon(G) be the number of Eulerian orientations, that is, the orientations where each vertex has in-degree equal to the out-degree. Counting Eulerian orientations has triggered considerable interest in combinatorics, computer science and statistical physics. Probably, the best known result is due to Lieb [10] who determined the asymptotic number of Eulerian orientations of large grid graphs. Schrijver [14] gave a lower bound on the number of Eulerian orientations in terms of the degree sequence. Welsh [17] observed that for a 44–regular graph the Tutte-polynomial evaluation |TG​(0,−2)||T_{G}(0,-2)| is exactly the number of Eulerian orientations since nowhere-zero Z3Z_{3}-flows and Eulerian orientations are in one-to-one correspondence for 44–regular graphs. Mihail and Winkler [12] gave an efficient randomized algorithm to sample and approximately count Eulerian orientations.

Let h⁡(G)h(G) denote the number of half graphs, that is, subgraphs FF such that dF​(v)=dG​(v)/2d_{F}(v)=d_{G}(v)/2 for each vertex vv. Note that h⁡(G)>0h(G)>0 if GG is not only Eulerian, but each of its connected component has an even number of edges. This condition is clearly necessary to have a half graph, and also sufficient: every second edge of an Eulerian tour will determine a half graph.

Recently, M. Borbényi and P. Csikvári [4] proved that ε⁡(G)≥h⁡(G)\varepsilon(G)\geq h(G) holds true for all Eulerian graphs with equality if and and only if GG is bipartite. In this paper we give a simple new proof of this fact, and we give identities and inequalities for the number of Eulerian orientations and half graphs of a 22-cover of a graph GG. In fact, we study the number of orientations and factors of 22-covers with prescribed in-degree and degree, respectively.

1.1. Results.

For an edge set A⊆E⁡(G)A\subseteq E(G) let ε⁡(A)\varepsilon(A) denote the number of Eulerian orientations of the graph (V,A)(V,A). Similarly, let h⁡(A)h(A) denote the number of half graphs of the graph (V,A)(V,A). Our first result is an identity for ε⁡(G)\varepsilon(G) and h⁡(G)h(G).

Theorem 1.1.

Let GG be an Eulerian graph with edge set EE. Then

ε​(G)2=∑A⊆Eε⁡(A)​ε​(E∖A)\varepsilon(G)^{2}=\sum_{A\subseteq E}\varepsilon(A)\varepsilon(E\setminus A)

and

h​(G)2=∑A⊆Eh⁡(A)​h​(E∖A).h(G)^{2}=\sum_{A\subseteq E}h(A)h(E\setminus A).

Using the identities of Theorem 1.1 we can easily give a new proof of the following theorem of M. Borbényi and P. Csikvári [4].

Theorem 1.2 (M. Borbényi and P. Csikvári [4]).

Let GG be an Eulerian graph. Then ε⁡(G)≥h⁡(G)\varepsilon(G)\geq h(G) with equality if and only if GG is bipartite.

As we will see it is natural to consider the number of Eulerian orientations and half graphs of 22-covers of an Eulerian graph GG.

Definition 1.3.

A kk-cover (or kk-lift) HH of a graph GG is defined as follows. The vertex set of HH is V⁡(H)=V⁡(G)×{0,1,…,k−1}V(H)=V(G)\times\{0,1,\dots,k-1\}, and if (u,v)∈E⁡(G)(u,v)\in E(G), then we choose a perfect matching between the vertices (u,i)(u,i) and (v,j)(v,j) for 0≤i,j≤k−10\leq i,j\leq k-1. If (u,v)∉E⁡(G)(u,v)\notin E(G), then there are no edges between (u,i)(u,i) and (v,j)(v,j) for 0≤i,j≤k−10\leq i,j\leq k-1.

When k=2k=2 one can encode the 22-lift HH by putting signs on the edges of the graph GG: the ++ sign means that we use the matching ((u,0),(v,0)),((u,1),(v,1))((u,0),(v,0)),((u,1),(v,1)) at the edge (u,v)(u,v), the −- sign means that we use the matching ((u,0),(v,1)),((u,1),(v,0))((u,0),(v,1)),((u,1),(v,0)) at the edge (u,v)(u,v). For instance, if we put ++ signs to every edge, then we simply get G∪GG\cup G as HH, and if we put −- signs everywhere, then the obtained 22-cover HH is simply G×K2G\times K_{2}. Observe that if GG is bipartite, then G∪G=G×K2G\cup G=G\times K_{2}, but other 22-covers might differ from G∪GG\cup G.

Graph cover techniques played important roles in the resolution of many open problems. A. Marcus, D. Spielmann and N. Srivastava [11] used graph covers to construct Ramanujan graphs. The idea was suggested by Y. Bilu and N. Linial [3]. Y. Zhao [19] used the bipartite double cover to prove a conjecture of N. Alon [2] and J. Kahn [9] on the number of independent sets. Later he developed his ideas in the paper [20]. N. Ruozzi [13] proved a conjecture of A. Sudderth, E. Wainwright, and M. Willsky [18] on the Bethe approximation of an attractive graphical model by building on an observation due to P. Vontobel [16] connecting graph covers with Bethe approximation. P. Csikvári [6] combined graph covers with graph limit theory to prove the so-called Lower Matching Conjecture of S. Friedland, E. Krop and K. Markström [7]. The properties of random lifts are also widely studied, see for instance the papers [1] and [8].

Theorem 1.4.

Let GG be an Eulerian graph with edge set EE. Then

ε⁡(G×K2)=h⁡(G×K2)=∑A⊆Eε⁡(A)​h​(E∖A).\varepsilon(G\times K_{2})=h(G\times K_{2})=\sum_{A\subseteq E}\varepsilon(A)h(E\setminus A).

Combining Theorem 1.4 with Theorem 1.2 we get that

ε⁡(G∪G)≥ε⁡(G×K2)=h⁡(G×K2)≥h⁡(G∪G).\varepsilon(G\cup G)\geq\varepsilon(G\times K_{2})=h(G\times K_{2})\geq h(G\cup G).

These inequalities can be generalized as follows. Let HH be an arbitrary 22-cover of an Eulerian graph GG. Then

ε⁡(G∪G)≥ε⁡(H)andh⁡(G×K2)≥h⁡(H).\varepsilon(G\cup G)\geq\varepsilon(H)\ \ \ \mbox{and}\ \ \ h(G\times K_{2})\geq h(H).

In fact, even more general statement is true. To spell out this generalization we need the concepts εr¯​(G)\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(G) and hr¯​(G)h_{\underline{r}}(G).

Definition 1.5.

Let r¯G=(rv)v∈V⁡(G)∈ℤV⁡(G)\underline{r}^{G}=(r_{v})_{v\in V(G)}\in\mathbb{Z}^{V(G)}. Let εr¯​(G)\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(G) denote the number of orientations of GG with in-degree rvr_{v} at vertex vv. We will call such an orientation an r¯\underline{r}-orientation.

Similarly, let hr¯​(G)h_{\underline{r}}(G) be the number of subgraphs FF of GG with degree dF​(v)=rvd_{F}(v)=r_{v} for each vertex vv. We will call such a subgraph an r¯\underline{r}-factor.

Clearly, if rv=dG​(v)/2r_{v}=d_{G}(v)/2 for each vertex vv, then εr¯​(G)=ε⁡(G)\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(G)=\varepsilon(G) and hr¯​(G)=h​(G)h_{\underline{r}}(G)=h(G). Other notable case is when rv=rr_{v}=r for all vv, then hr¯​(G)h_{\underline{r}}(G) counts the number of rr-factors.

Definition 1.6.

Let r¯G=(rv)v∈V⁡(G)∈ℤV⁡(G)\underline{r}^{G}=(r_{v})_{v\in V(G)}\in\mathbb{Z}^{V(G)} and let HH be a kk-cover of GG. We say that r¯H=(rv)v∈V⁡(H)∈ℤV⁡(H)\underline{r}^{H}=(r_{v})_{v\in V(H)}\in\mathbb{Z}^{V(H)} is induced by r¯G\underline{r}^{G} if ru′=rur_{u^{\prime}}=r_{u} for all lifts u′∈V⁡(H)u^{\prime}\in V(H) of u∈V⁡(G)u\in V(G).

In the following statements we can even drop the condition of GG being Eulerian.

Theorem 1.7.

Let r¯G=(rv)v∈V⁡(G)∈ℤV⁡(G)\underline{r}^{G}=(r_{v})_{v\in V(G)}\in\mathbb{Z}^{V(G)}. Let HH be an arbitrary 22-cover of the graph GG. Let us denote by r¯\underline{r} the induced vector of r¯G\underline{r}^{G} on HH and G∪GG\cup G. Then

εr¯​(G∪G)≥εr¯​(H).\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(G\cup G)\geq\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(H).
Theorem 1.8.

Let r¯G=(rv)v∈V⁡(G)∈ℤV⁡(G)\underline{r}^{G}=(r_{v})_{v\in V(G)}\in\mathbb{Z}^{V(G)}. Let HH be an arbitrary 22-cover of a graph GG. Let us denote by r¯\underline{r} the induced vector of r¯G\underline{r}^{G} on HH and G×K2G\times K_{2}. Then

hr¯​(G×K2)≥hr¯​(H).h_{\underline{r}}(G\times K_{2})\geq h_{\underline{r}}(H).

Note that Theorems 1.7 and 1.8 provide yet another proof of Theorem 1.2 by

ε​(G)2=ε⁡(G∪G)≥ε⁡(G×K2)=h⁡(G×K2)≥h⁡(G∪G)=h​(G)2.\varepsilon(G)^{2}=\varepsilon(G\cup G)\geq\varepsilon(G\times K_{2})=h(G\times K_{2})\geq h(G\cup G)=h(G)^{2}.

Next we generalize the concept of Eulerian orientations and half graphs. To every edge of GG assign either oo or ss, that is, orientation or subgraph. Then for all edge we have two choices: if we assigned oo to the edge, then we need to orient it, so we choose one of the end points and add 11 to it, and add 00 to the other endpoint. (More precisely, we consider the in-degree.) If we assigned ss for the edge, then we need to decide whether we put this edge into subgraph or not, so we either add 11 to both endpoints, or add 00 to both endpoints. We will call such a configuration a factorientation. We will call the contribution of the edges to the vertex vv the mixed degree of vv, that is, it is the sum of the in-degree from oriented edges and the degree coming from the subgraph. After we choose oo or ss for every edge, we say that a factorientation is balanced, if for every vertex vv the mixed degree is dG​(v)/2d_{G}(v)/2. Let g⁡(G)g(G) be the number of balanced factorientations. We can see that this is a generalization of both Eulerian orientations and half graphs, because if we assign oo to each edge, then g⁡(G)=ε⁡(G)g(G)=\varepsilon(G) and if we assign ss to each edge, then g⁡(G)=h⁡(G)g(G)=h(G).

Theorem 1.9.

Let HH be a 2-cover of G=(V,E)G=(V,E) encoded with ++ and −- signs, such that for each edge the 22-lifts of this edge get the same letter (oo or ss). For an edge subset B⊆EB\subseteq E let B¯\overline{B} denote the graph with vertex set VV and edge set BB, just for each edge with a minus in it we swap oo to ss and vice versa. Then

g⁡(H)=∑A⊆Eg⁡(A)​g​(E∖A¯).g(H)=\sum_{A\subseteq E}g(A)g(\overline{E\setminus A}).

Clearly, Theorem 1.1 and 1.4 are corollaries of this theorem. We can also generalize Theorem 1.2 as follows.

Theorem 1.10.

Let GG be an Eulerian graph with oo and ss assignments on the edges. Let g⁡(G)g(G) be the number of corresponding balanced factorientations. Then g⁡(G)≤ε⁡(G)g(G)\leq\varepsilon(G).

With the method that we use to prove Theorem 1.1 we can also prove another nice result about orientations:

Theorem 1.11.

Let GG be an Eulerian graph. Then εr¯​(G)\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(G) is maximal if rv=dG​(v)2r_{v}=\frac{d_{G}(v)}{2} for all vertex vv.

1.2. Organization of this paper and notations.

In the next section we prove Theorems 1.1, 1.2 and 1.4. In Section 3 we prove Theorem 1.7 and Theorem 1.8. In Section 4 we prove Theorems 1.9 and 1.10. Then we prove Theorem 1.11. We end the paper with an open problem.

Notations. For a graph GG and a vertex vv let EvE_{v} denote the edges incident to vv in the graph GG and let dG​(v)=|Ev|d_{G}(v)=|E_{v}|. Furthermore, NG​(v)N_{G}(v) denotes the set of neighbors of vv. For a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) let pm⁡(G)\mathrm{pm}(G) denote the number of perfect matchings. If HH is a 22-cover of GG, then V0V_{0} and V1V_{1} will denote the two copies of the vertex set. In particular, G×K2G\times K_{2} is a bipartite graph with bipartite classes V0V_{0} and V1V_{1}. For a vertex u∈V⁡(G)u\in V(G) let u0u_{0} and u1u_{1} denote the two copies of uu in the 22-cover HH.

2. Proof of Theorems 1.1, 1.2 and 1.4

In this section we prove Theorems 1.1, 1.2 and 1.4.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

We only prove the identity h​(G)2=∑A⊆Eh⁡(A)​h​(E∖A)h(G)^{2}=\sum_{A\subseteq E}h(A)h(E\setminus A). The proof of the other identity is very similar. Consider S,T⊆E⁡(G)S,T\subseteq E(G) determining two half graphs. Let A=S​Δ​TA=S\Delta T be the symmetric difference of the half graphs SS and TT. Let B=E∖AB=E\setminus A, then B=(S∩T)∪(E∖(S∪T))B=(S\cap T)\cup(E\setminus(S\cup T)). Recall that EvE_{v} denotes the edges incident to the vertex vv. Since |S∩Ev|=|T∩Ev|=dG​(v)/2|S\cap E_{v}|=|T\cap E_{v}|=d_{G}(v)/2 we have |Ev∩(A∩S)|=|Ev∩(A∩T)||E_{v}\cap(A\cap S)|=|E_{v}\cap(A\cap T)| and |Ev∩(S∩T)|=|Ev∩(E∖(S∪T)||E_{v}\cap(S\cap T)|=|E_{v}\cap(E\setminus(S\cup T)|. In other words, A∩SA\cap S is a half graph of AA, and B∩(S∩T)B\cap(S\cap T) is a half graph of BB. Clearly, SS and TT determine A,A∩S,B,B∩(S∩T)A,A\cap S,B,B\cap(S\cap T). But it is also true that A,A∩S,B,B∩(S∩T)A,A\cap S,B,B\cap(S\cap T) determine SS and TT since S=(A∩S)∪(S∩T)S=(A\cap S)\cup(S\cap T) and T=(A∩T)∪(S∩T)T=(A\cap T)\cup(S\cap T). The number of quadruple A,A∩S,B,B∩(S∩T)A,A\cap S,B,B\cap(S\cap T) is clearly ∑A⊆Eh⁡(A)​h​(E∖A)\sum_{A\subseteq E}h(A)h(E\setminus A). Hence

h​(G)2=∑A⊆Eh⁡(A)​h​(E∖A).h(G)^{2}=\sum_{A\subseteq E}h(A)h(E\setminus A).

In case of Eulerian orientations let SS and TT be two Eulerian orientations, and let AA be the set of edges where the orientations coincide and B=E∖AB=E\setminus A be the remaining edges. Similarly to the previous discussion SS restricted to AA and BB gives an Eulerian orientation. The rest of the proof is the same. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

The proof is very similar to the proof of Theorem 1.1. Since G×K2=(V0,V1,E)G\times K_{2}=(V_{0},V_{1},E) is bipartite we have ε⁡(G×K2)=h⁡(G×K2)\varepsilon(G\times K_{2})=h(G\times K_{2}). Consider a half graph SS of G×K2G\times K_{2}. Let π:G×K2→G\pi:G\times K_{2}\to G be the natural projection. For k=0,1,2k=0,1,2 let Ak={e∈E||π−1​(e)∩S|=k}A_{k}=\{e\in E\ |\ |\pi^{-1}(e)\cap S|=k\}. Since SS was a half graph of G×K2G\times K_{2} we get that for each vertex vv we have |Ev∩A0|=|Ev∩A2||E_{v}\cap A_{0}|=|E_{v}\cap A_{2}|. In other words, A0A_{0} is a half graph of A0∪A2A_{0}\cup A_{2}. Let us orient an edge (u,v)∈A1(u,v)\in A_{1} from uu to vv if (u0,v1)∈S(u_{0},v_{1})\in S. Since SS was a half graph of G×K2G\times K_{2} this gives an Eulerian orientation of the edges of A1A_{1}. Clearly, from the Eulerian orientation of A1A_{1} and the half graph A0A_{0} of A0∪A2A_{0}\cup A_{2} we can immediately reconstruct SS. Hence

h⁡(G×K2)=∑A1⊆Eε⁡(A1)​h​(A0∪A2)=∑A⊆Eε⁡(A)​h​(E∖A).h(G\times K_{2})=\sum_{A_{1}\subseteq E}\varepsilon(A_{1})h(A_{0}\cup A_{2})=\sum_{A\subseteq E}\varepsilon(A)h(E\setminus A).

∎

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

We prove the statement by induction on the number of edges of GG. If the graph has no edge, then the statement is trivial. If it consists of a single cycle of length kk together with isolated vertices, then ε⁡(G)=2\varepsilon(G)=2 and h⁡(G)=0h(G)=0 or 22 depending on kk being odd or even. So in this case the theorem is true. If GG is different from a single cycle together with isolated vertices, then we use induction:

ε​(G)2−2​ε​(G)=∑A⊆EA≠∅,Eε⁡(A)​ε​(E∖A)≥∑A⊆EA≠∅,Eh⁡(A)​h​(E∖A)=h​(G)2−2​h​(G).\varepsilon(G)^{2}-2\varepsilon(G)=\sum_{A\subseteq E\atop A\neq\emptyset,E}\varepsilon(A)\varepsilon(E\setminus A)\geq\sum_{A\subseteq E\atop A\neq\emptyset,E}h(A)h(E\setminus A)=h(G)^{2}-2h(G).

Since ε⁡(G)≥1\varepsilon(G)\geq 1 and the function x2−2​xx^{2}-2x is a monotone increasing function for x≥1x\geq 1 we get that ε⁡(G)≥h⁡(G)\varepsilon(G)\geq h(G). ∎

3. Proof of Theorems 1.7 and  1.8

In this section we prove Theorems 1.7 and  1.8. The proofs rely on three observations, one of them is due to A. Schrijver relating the number of r¯\underline{r}-orientations of a graph GG to the number of perfect matchings of a certain bipartite graph G∗G^{*} constructed from GG. (In fact, we will slightly modify it, but still attribute it to A. Schrijver.) A similar observation connects the number of r¯\underline{r}-factors of a graph GG to the number of perfect matchings of another graph G∗⁣∗G^{**} constructed from GG. The last observation is due to P. Csikvári and gives an inequality between the number of perfect matchings of certain 22-covers of a graph GG.

Lemma 3.1 (A. Schrijver [14]).

Let GG be a graph, and let G∗G^{*} be the following bipartite graph. On one side of the bipartite graph every vertex corresponds to an edge e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G). On the other side of the bipartite graph we take rvr_{v} copies of each vertex vv. Finally, an edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v) is adjacent to all copies of uu and vv. Then

pm⁡(G∗)=εr¯​(G)​∏v∈V⁡(G)rv!.\mathrm{pm}(G^{*})=\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(G)\prod_{v\in V(G)}r_{v}!.
Proof.

Let R=∏v∈V⁡(G)rv!R=\prod_{v\in V(G)}r_{v}!. There is an 11 to RR map from the set of r¯\underline{r}-orientations to the set of perfect matchings of G∗G^{*}. Namely, if the edges (u,vi)∈E⁡(G)(u,v_{i})\in E(G) for i=1,…​rui=1,\dots r_{u} are oriented towards uu, then we take the union of perfect matchings between eu​vie_{uv_{i}} and the rur_{u} copies of uu to get a perfect matching of G∗G^{*}. ∎

A similar lemma enable us to encode hr¯h_{\underline{r}} via perfect matchings. A qualitative version of this lemma appeared in [15].

Lemma 3.2 (W. Tutte [15]).

Let GG be a graph, and let G∗⁣∗G^{**} be the following graph. For each edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v) we introduce two vertices eu​ve_{uv} and ev​ue_{vu}, and for each vertex vv we introduce rvr_{v} copies of vv. Then we connect eu​ve_{uv} with ev​ue_{vu}, and we also connect the rur_{u} copies of uu with ev​ue_{vu} for each v∈NG​(u)v\in N_{G}(u). Then

pm⁡(G∗⁣∗)=hr¯​(G)​∏v∈V⁡(G)rv!.\mathrm{pm}(G^{**})=h_{\underline{r}}(G)\prod_{v\in V(G)}r_{v}!.
Proof.

Let R=∏v∈V⁡(G)rv!R=\prod_{v\in V(G)}r_{v}!. Again there is an 11 to RR map from the set of r¯\underline{r}-factors to the set of perfect matchings of G∗⁣∗G^{**}. Namely, if the edges (u,vi)∈E⁡(G)(u,v_{i})\in E(G) for i=1,…​rui=1,\dots r_{u} are in the r¯\underline{r}-factor, then to get a perfect matching of G∗⁣∗G^{**}, we take the union of perfect matchings between evi​ue_{v_{i}u} and the rur_{u} copies of uu together with those edges (ex​y,ey​x)(e_{xy},e_{yx}) for which (x,y)∈E⁡(G)(x,y)\in E(G), but is not in the r¯\underline{r}-factor. ∎

Next we need a lemma that relates perfect matchings with covers.

Lemma 3.3 (P. Csikvári [6, 5]).

Let GG be a graph, and let HH be an arbitrary 22-cover of GG. Then

pm⁡(H)≤pm⁡(G×K2).\mathrm{pm}(H)\leq\mathrm{pm}(G\times K_{2}).

In particular, if GG is bipartite, then pm⁡(H)≤pm​(G)2\mathrm{pm}(H)\leq\mathrm{pm}(G)^{2}.

Sketch of the proof.

Let us project the edges of a perfect matching of a 22-cover HH to the graph GG. The obtained configuration consists of cycles and double-edges, that is, two edges projected to the same edge. (Every degree must be 22 in the obtained configuration.) For such a configuration we can count the number of preimages. Each cycle can be lifted in at most 22 ways since the preimage of one edge determines the preimage of the subsequent edges in the cycle. It may occur though that we cannot close the cycle. (This happens for instance if try to lift a 33-cycle in the union of two 33-cycles.) On the other hand, it is easy to see that on G×K2G\times K_{2} every cycle can be lifted in exactly 22 ways. This means that every configuration has at least as many preimages on G×K2G\times K_{2} than on another 22-cover HH.

∎

Proof of Theorem 1.7.

Let HH be an arbitrary cover of the graph GG. Let us construct the bipartite graphs G∗G^{*} and H∗H^{*} of Lemma 3.1. Observe that H∗H^{*} is also a 22-cover of G∗G^{*}, and so by Lemma 3.3 we have pm​(G∗)2≥pm⁡(H∗)\mathrm{pm}(G^{*})^{2}\geq\mathrm{pm}(H^{*}). Using Lemma 3.1 we have

pm​(G∗)2=εr¯​(G)2​(∏v∈V⁡(G)rv!)2\mathrm{pm}(G^{*})^{2}=\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(G)^{2}\left(\prod_{v\in V(G)}r_{v}!\right)^{2}

and

pm⁡(H∗)=εr¯​(H)​∏v∈V⁡(H)rv!=εr¯​(H)​(∏v∈V⁡(G)rv!)2.\mathrm{pm}(H^{*})=\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(H)\prod_{v\in V(H)}r_{v}!=\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(H)\left(\prod_{v\in V(G)}r_{v}!\right)^{2}.

Hence εr¯​(G)2≥εr¯​(H)\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(G)^{2}\geq\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(H). ∎

Remark 3.4.

An interesting application of Theorem 1.7 is the following. Let Tn,mT_{n,m} be the toroidal grid of size n×mn\times m, that is, a grid of size n×mn\times m closed in a toroidal way to make it 44-regular. Then ε⁡(Tn,m)≥(43)3​n​m/2\varepsilon(T_{n,m})\geq\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^{3nm/2}. This can can be seen as follows. E. Lieb [10] showed that limn,m→∞ε​(Tn,m)1/n​m=(43)3/2\lim_{n,m\to\infty}\varepsilon(T_{n,m})^{1/nm}=\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^{3/2}. On the other hand, T2​n,mT_{2n,m} and Tn,2​mT_{n,2m} are 22-covers of Tn,mT_{n,m} so ε​(Tn,m)2≥ε⁡(T2​n,m)\varepsilon(T_{n,m})^{2}\geq\varepsilon(T_{2n,m}) and ε⁡(Tn,2​m)\varepsilon(T_{n,2m}) so it is necessary that ε​(Tn,m)1/n​m≥(43)3/2\varepsilon(T_{n,m})^{1/nm}\geq\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^{3/2} for every n,mn,m.

Proof of Theorem 1.8.

Let HH be an arbitrary cover of the graph GG. Let us construct the bipartite graphs G∗⁣∗G^{**} and H∗⁣∗H^{**} of Lemma 3.2. Observe that H∗⁣∗H^{**} is also a 22-cover of G∗⁣∗G^{**}, and (G×K2)∗⁣∗=G∗⁣∗×K2(G\times K_{2})^{**}=G^{**}\times K_{2} and so by Lemma 3.3 we have pm⁡((G×K2)∗⁣∗)≥pm⁡(H∗⁣∗)\mathrm{pm}((G\times K_{2})^{**})\geq\mathrm{pm}(H^{**}). Using Lemma 3.2 we have

pm⁡((G×K2)∗⁣∗)=hr¯​(G×K2)​∏v∈V⁡(G×K2)rv!=hr¯​(G×K2)​(∏v∈V⁡(G)rv!)2\mathrm{pm}((G\times K_{2})^{**})=h_{\underline{r}}(G\times K_{2})\prod_{v\in V(G\times K_{2})}r_{v}!=h_{\underline{r}}(G\times K_{2})\left(\prod_{v\in V(G)}r_{v}!\right)^{2}

and

pm⁡(H∗⁣∗)=hr¯​(H)​∏v∈V⁡(H)rv!=hr¯​(H)​(∏v∈V⁡(G)rv!)2.\mathrm{pm}(H^{**})=h_{\underline{r}}(H)\prod_{v\in V(H)}r_{v}!=h_{\underline{r}}(H)\left(\prod_{v\in V(G)}r_{v}!\right)^{2}.

Hence hr¯​(G×K2)≥hr¯​(H)h_{\underline{r}}(G\times K_{2})\geq h_{\underline{r}}(H).

∎

4. general 2-cover

In this section we prove Theorems 1.9 and  1.10.

Proof of Theorem 1.9.

Consider a balanced factorientation SS of the graph HH. Take the natural projection from HH to GG, and let AA be the set of edges for which the projected edges coincide, that is, both edges are oriented in the same way if there is an oo on that edge, or they are both or neither in the subgraph if there is an ss on that edge.

Let B=E∖AB=E\setminus A. The factorientation SS was balanced so for all vertex vv the mixed degrees of v0v_{0} and v1v_{1} are both dG​(v)/2d_{G}(v)/2. This means that after the natural projection – and the doubling of the original edges of the graph– the mixed degree of vertex vv is dG​(v)d_{G}(v). If an edge is in AA, then it contributes either 00 or 22 to the mixed degree of vv, otherwise it contributes 11. Thus there must be equal number of 00’s and 22’s contributions, which means that if we restrict the graph to AA, then we also get a balanced factorientation.

For an edge (u,v)∈B(u,v)\in B if (u,v)(u,v) has a plus sign on it, then it contributes the same amount to the mixed degree of uu and vv as it contributed to the mixed degrees of u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} with the edge (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) in SS.

If (u,v)(u,v) has a minus sign on it, then in (u,v)(u,v) change ss to oo and vice verse. If it was oo before and the orientations were u0→v1u_{0}\to v_{1} and v0→u1v_{0}\to u_{1}, then we do not put the edge (u,v)(u,v) into the subgraph. If it was oo before and the orientations were u1→v0u_{1}\to v_{0} and v1→u0v_{1}\to u_{0}, then we do put the edge (u,v)(u,v) into the subgraph. Note that the contribution of these edges to the mixed degree of a vertex uu is the same as the contribution of the original edges to the vertex u0u_{0}.

Similarly, if it was a ss before, and (u0,v1)(u_{0},v_{1}) was in the subgraph, but (u1,v0)(u_{1},v_{0}) was not, then orient the edge uu from v0v_{0} to u0u_{0}. This way it is again true that the contribution of these edges to the mixed degree of a vertex uu is the same as the contribution of the original edges to the vertex u0u_{0}.

So for all (u,v)∈B(u,v)\in B we made sure that the contribution of the orientation or factor to the mixed degree of a vertex uu is the same contribution as the original edges to the mixed degree of the vertex u0u_{0}. Finally, observe that since the mixed degree of u0u_{0} and u1u_{1} was the same, and the edges of AA contributed the same to the mixed degrees, it is necessary that the mixed degree contributed by the edges of BB to the vertex uu is exactly dB​(u)/2d_{B}(u)/2. This means that the constructed factorientation is balanced if we restrict to the edges of BB.

Finally, observe that if we get a balanced factorientation of AA and E∖A¯\overline{E\setminus A} then we can easily get back the balanced factorientation of HH. This finishes the proof. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.10.

The proof is practically the same as the proof of Theorem 1.2. We use induction to the number of edges. We have

g​(G)2=g⁡(G∪G)=∑A⊆Eg⁡(A)​g​(E∖A¯)=∑A⊆Eg⁡(A)​g​(E∖A)g(G)^{2}=g(G\cup G)=\sum_{A\subseteq E}g(A)g(\overline{E\setminus A})=\sum_{A\subseteq E}g(A)g(E\setminus A)

since G∪GG\cup G corresponds to the 22-cover with only ++ signs. By induction we have
g⁡(A)≤ε⁡(A)g(A)\leq\varepsilon(A) if A≠EA\neq E. Hence g​(G)2−2​g​(G)≤ε​(G)2−2​ε​(G)g(G)^{2}-2g(G)\leq\varepsilon(G)^{2}-2\varepsilon(G) which implies that g⁡(G)≤ε⁡(G)g(G)\leq\varepsilon(G). ∎

5. Proof of Theorem 1.11

In this section we prove Theorem 1.11.

Proof of Theorem 1.11.

We prove the statement by induction on the number of edges. The statement is true for cycles.

Let r¯∈ℤV⁡(G)\underline{r}\in\mathbb{Z}^{V(G)} be an arbitrary vector and let d¯∈ℤV⁡(G)\underline{d}\in\mathbb{Z}^{V(G)} be the vector where dv=dG​(v)d_{v}=d_{G}(v). Notice that εr¯​(G)=εd¯−r¯​(G)\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(G)=\varepsilon_{\underline{d}-\underline{r}}(G) because if we change the direction of all edges in an r¯\underline{r}-orientation then we get a (d¯−r¯)(\underline{d}-\underline{r})-orientation. So it is enough to prove, that

εr¯​(G)​εd¯−r¯​(G)≤εd¯/2​(G)2\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(G)\varepsilon_{\underline{d}-\underline{r}}(G)\leq\varepsilon_{\underline{d}/2}(G)^{2}

Consider S,T⊆E⁡(G)S,T\subseteq E(G) determining an r¯\underline{r}-orientation and a (d¯−r¯)(\underline{d}-\underline{r})-orientation respectively. Let A⊆EA\subseteq E be the set of edges where the two orientations coincide, and let B=E∖AB=E\setminus A be the remaining edges. We claim that A∩SA\cap S is an Eulerian orientation of AA. To see this consider a vertex vv of GG. The sum of in-degrees of vv in SS and TT is dG​(v)d_{G}(v) so among the edges where SS and TT coincide there must be equal number of edges which point to vv and which start from vv. This is true for all vertex vv of GG so A∩SA\cap S is an Eulerian orientation of AA. From this it is easy to see that S∩BS\cap B is an (r¯−dA¯/2)(\underline{r}-\underline{d_{A}}/2)-orientation of BB. If we choose S∩BS\cap B that determines T∩BT\cap B so

εr¯​(G)​εd¯−r¯​(G)=∑A⊆Eε⁡(A)​εr¯−dA¯/2​(E∖A)\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(G)\varepsilon_{\underline{d}-\underline{r}}(G)=\sum_{A\subseteq E}\varepsilon(A)\varepsilon_{\underline{r}-\underline{d_{A}}/2}(E\setminus A)

The degree of a vertex vv in E∖AE\setminus A is dG​(v)−dA​(v)d_{G}(v)-d_{A}(v) so from induction we know that εr¯−dA¯/2​(E∖A)≤εd¯/2−dA¯/2​(E∖A)\varepsilon_{\underline{r}-\underline{d_{A}}/2}(E\setminus A)\leq\varepsilon_{\underline{d}/2-\underline{d_{A}}/2}(E\setminus A) if A≠∅A\neq\emptyset so

εr¯​(G)​εd¯−r¯​(G)−εr¯​(G)=∑A⊆EA≠∅ε⁡(A)​εr¯−dA¯/2​(E∖A)≤\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(G)\varepsilon_{\underline{d}-\underline{r}}(G)-\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(G)=\sum_{A\subseteq E\atop A\neq\emptyset}\varepsilon(A)\varepsilon_{\underline{r}-\underline{d_{A}}/2}(E\setminus A)\leq
≤∑A⊆EA≠∅ε⁡(A)​εd¯/2−dA¯/2​(E∖A)=εd¯/2​(G)2−εd¯/2​(G)\leq\sum_{A\subseteq E\atop A\neq\emptyset}\varepsilon(A)\varepsilon_{\underline{d}/2-\underline{d_{A}}/2}(E\setminus A)=\varepsilon_{\underline{d}/2}(G)^{2}-\varepsilon_{\underline{d}/2}(G)

so

εr¯​(G)​εd¯−r¯​(G)≤εd¯/2​(G)2\varepsilon_{\underline{r}}(G)\varepsilon_{\underline{d}-\underline{r}}(G)\leq\varepsilon_{\underline{d}/2}(G)^{2}

∎

6. Open problem

We end this paper with an open problem.

Conjecture 6.1.

Let GG be an Eulerian graph, and let HH be a kk-cover of GG. Then ε​(G)k≥ε⁡(H)\varepsilon(G)^{k}\geq\varepsilon(H).
